claim: Flies detect odors with their antennae and maxillary palps, which together contain ~1300 olfactory-receptor neurons (ORNs).
source: Flies detect odors with their antennae and maxillary palps, which together contain ~1300 olfactory-receptor neurons (ORNs) (Lai et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lai et al., 2008.

claim: The odor-response profile of each adult ORN is determined by one of ~45 possible receptor types.
source: The odor-response profile of each adult ORN is determined by one of ~45 possible receptor types (Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Gomez-Diaz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005 and Gomez-Diaz et al., 2018.

claim: ORNs sharing the same receptor type converge on a glomerulus in the antennal lobe, where they synapse with local interneurons (LNs) and projection neurons (PNs).
source: ORNs sharing the same receptor type converge on a glomerulus in the antennal lobe, where they synapse with local interneurons (LNs) and projection neurons (PNs) (Couto et al., 2005; Gao et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Couto et al., 2005 and Gao et al., 2000.

claim: The LNs facilitate both excitatory and inhibitory interactions between glomeruli.
source: Innervating throughout the antennal lobe and connecting multiple glomeruli, the LNs facilitate both excitatory and inhibitory interactions between glomeruli (Groschner and Miesenböck, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Groschner and Miesenböck, 2019.

claim: Modified information from the antennal lobe is relayed by the PNs to higher brain centers, namely mushroom bodies and the lateral horn.
source: This modified information is relayed by the PNs to higher brain centers, namely mushroom bodies and the lateral horn (Lai et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lai et al., 2008, Wang et al., 2014, and Wong et al., 2002.

claim: A subset of receptors respond specifically to single odorants, and their ORNs individually drive innate valence.
source: At least some ORN-driven behaviors appear to follow simple rules: a subset of receptors respond specifically to single odorants, and their ORNs individually drive innate valence (Ache and Young, 2005; Grabe and Sachse, 2018; Haddad et al., 2010; Haverkamp et al., 2018; Stensmyr et al., 2012; Suh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Acutely tuned, strongly valent ORN classes include neurons tuned to danger (e.g. toxic odorants) and pheromones.
source: These acutely tuned, strongly valent ORN classes include neurons tuned to danger (e.g. toxic odorants) and pheromones.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about labeled lines in olfactory systems.

claim: Many olfactory receptors are broadly tuned to respond to many odorants, and most pure odorants evoke responses across many ORN classes.
source: Unlike labeled lines, many other olfactory receptors are broadly tuned to respond to many odorants, and most pure odorants evoke responses across many ORN classes (Hallem and Carlson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hallem and Carlson, 2006.

claim: Gr66a-Gal4 labels bitter-taste-sensing gustatory-receptor neurons.
source: We tested the validity of this approach with flies expressing the Chr channel under the control of the Gr66a-Gal4 driver line, which labels bitter-taste-sensing gustatory-receptor neurons (Moon et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moon et al., 2006.

claim: Gr66a-neuron activation has been previously reported to drive avoidance when artificially activated.
source: which labels bitter-taste-sensing gustatory-receptor neurons (Moon et al., 2006) and has been previously reported to drive avoidance when artificially activated (Aso et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014 and Shao et al., 2017.

claim: Experimental Gr66a > Chr flies displayed robust light avoidance.
source: In a sequence of 12 trials using three light intensities (14, 42, and 70 μW/mm2) and two airflow states (on/off), the experimental Gr66a > Chr flies displayed robust light avoidance (Figure 1B–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in multiple figures.

claim: The standardized effect size of Gr66a-neuron avoidance at the highest intensity was Cohen's d = –2.70 at 70 μW/mm2.
source: the standardized effect size of Gr66a-neuron avoidance at the highest intensity (Cohen's d = –2.70 at 70 μW/mm2) was almost as large as that of the previously reported valence response (d = –3.63; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to prior studies.

claim: Orco-Gal4 labels ~70% of all ORNs.
source: To benchmark attraction behavior, we used an Orco-Gal4 driver line that labels ~70% of all ORNs (Larsson et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Larsson et al., 2004 and Wang et al., 2003.

claim: One prior study showed no behavioral effect of Orco-neuron activation.
source: Others have reported Orco-neuron valence results: one study showed no behavioral effect Suh et al., 2007
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suh et al., 2007.

claim: Another prior study found Orco-neuron attraction in the presence of a wind cue only.
source: another found attraction in the presence of a wind cue only Bell and Wilson, 2016.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bell and Wilson, 2016.

claim: At two higher light intensities (42 and 70 μW/mm2), Orco > Chr flies exhibited pronounced attraction even in still air.
source: In our experiments, at two higher light intensities (42 and 70 μW/mm2), Orco > Chr flies exhibited pronounced attraction even in still air (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in figures.

claim: The valence of Orco-neuron activation was typically stronger than that reported in prior studies (e.g. d = 0.56 in still air in this study versus d ≤ 0.10).
source: The valence was typically stronger than that reported in prior studies (e.g. d = 0.56 in still air in this study versus d ≤ 0.10), establishing assay sensitivity for attraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data to prior studies.

claim: Changing the temporal sequence of the 12 trials had negligible effects on Orco-neuron positive valence.
source: Changing the temporal sequence of the 12 trials had negligible effects on Orco-neuron positive valence, suggesting that valence is not greatly susceptible to order bias, for example, due to habituation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in a figure supplement.

claim: Using available Gal4 lines, 46 receptor classes were assessed for optogenetic valence.
source: Using available Gal4 lines, each driving expression in a single ORN type, we assessed the optogenetic valence of 46 receptor classes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The empirical Bayes analysis identified 10 valent classes: six ORNs elicited attraction and four elicited aversion.
source: The empirical Bayes analysis identified 10 valent classes: six ORNs elicited attraction and four elicited aversion (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis results presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Or56a is the receptor for the aversive odorant geosmin.
source: Four are considered labeled lines: Or56a, the receptor for the aversive odorant geosmin; Gr21a, the receptor for the aversive odorant carbon dioxide; Or67d, the receptor for the pheromone 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate; and Or47b, which senses the pheromone palmitoleic acid (Davis, 2007; Jones et al., 2007; Kurtovic et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2016; Stensmyr et al., 2012; Suh et al., 2004; van der Goes van Naters and Carlson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Gr21a is the receptor for the aversive odorant carbon dioxide.
source: Four are considered labeled lines: Or56a, the receptor for the aversive odorant geosmin; Gr21a, the receptor for the aversive odorant carbon dioxide; Or67d, the receptor for the pheromone 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate; and Or47b, which senses the pheromone palmitoleic acid (Davis, 2007; Jones et al., 2007; Kurtovic et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2016; Stensmyr et al., 2012; Suh et al., 2004; van der Goes van Naters and Carlson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Or67d is the receptor for the pheromone 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate.
source: Four are considered labeled lines: Or56a, the receptor for the aversive odorant geosmin; Gr21a, the receptor for the aversive odorant carbon dioxide; Or67d, the receptor for the pheromone 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate; and Or47b, which senses the pheromone palmitoleic acid (Davis, 2007; Jones et al., 2007; Kurtovic et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2016; Stensmyr et al., 2012; Suh et al., 2004; van der Goes van Naters and Carlson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Or47b senses the pheromone palmitoleic acid.
source: Four are considered labeled lines: Or56a, the receptor for the aversive odorant geosmin; Gr21a, the receptor for the aversive odorant carbon dioxide; Or67d, the receptor for the pheromone 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate; and Or47b, which senses the pheromone palmitoleic acid (Davis, 2007; Jones et al., 2007; Kurtovic et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2016; Stensmyr et al., 2012; Suh et al., 2004; van der Goes van Naters and Carlson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Or83c mediates attraction to farnesol, an odorant produced by some ripe fruits.
source: Additionally, Or83c mediates attraction to farnesol, an odorant produced by some ripe fruits (Ronderos et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ronderos et al., 2014.

claim: Or42b mediates attraction to vinegar.
source: while Or42b mediates attraction to vinegar (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Semmelhack and Wang, 2009.

claim: The screen successfully recaptured six ORN types already known to be involved in ecologically relevant valence functions.
source: Given that this screen successfully recaptured six ORN types already known to be involved in ecologically relevant valence functions, we consider that the screen was valid and sensitive.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results matching prior knowledge.

claim: The majority of the hits being ORNs with already-established valence implies that most ORNs are not singly valent.
source: Furthermore, the majority of the hits being ORNs with already-established valence implies that most ORNs are not singly valent.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Male flies exhibited strong responses to Orco-neuron activation, while females showed no response.
source: Although male flies exhibited strong responses to Orco-neuron activation, females showed no response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing male and female flies.

claim: The lack of response in female flies to Orco-neuron activation turned into a strong attraction when they were starved.
source: Surprisingly, this lack of response in females turned into a strong attraction when they were starved (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in a figure supplement.

claim: Activation of Or47b neurons (sensors of an aphrodisiac pheromone) was attractive to males, while females were indifferent.
source: Only one pheromone-receptor class showed sexual dimorphism: activation of Or47b neurons (sensors of an aphrodisiac pheromone) was attractive to males, while females were indifferent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing male and female responses.

claim: In isolation, most ORN classes do not drive valence.
source: Together, these results indicate that in isolation, most ORN classes do not drive valence.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Wind has been previously reported to be essential for the optogenetic valence of Orco neurons.
source: It has been previously reported that wind is essential for the optogenetic valence of Orco neurons (Bell and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bell and Wilson, 2016.

claim: With a lone exception (wind rendered Or59b valence more aversive in the lowest light intensity only), an empirical-Bayes model found that the wind effect sizes were indistinguishable from noise.
source: With a lone exception (wind rendered Or59b valence more aversive in the lowest light intensity only), an empirical-Bayes model found that the wind effect sizes were indistinguishable from noise (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis results presented in figures.

claim: Wind has essentially no impact on single ORN type-elicited behavior in walking flies.
source: Contradicting our hypothesis, this result indicates that wind has essentially no impact on single ORN type-elicited behavior in walking flies.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Chemosensory behaviors are influenced by an animal's internal energy state.
source: Chemosensory behaviors—for example gustatory and olfactory responses—are influenced by an animal's internal energy state.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Low internal energy can sensitize food odor-responsive ORNs and drive foraging.
source: Low internal energy, for example, can sensitize food odor-responsive ORNs and drive foraging (LeDue et al., 2016; Sengupta, 2013; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Starvation did not enhance attraction in the ORN valence assay.
source: Surprisingly, starvation did not enhance attraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Starvation reduced the responses triggered by three otherwise attractive ORNs: Or42b, Or47a, and Or83c.
source: On the contrary, it reduced the responses triggered by three otherwise attractive ORNs: Or42b, Or47a, and Or83c (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Starvation shifted the otherwise neutral valences of Or85f and Or49a, two receptors involved in sensing wasp odors, into aversion.
source: Starvation also shifted the otherwise neutral valences of Or85f and Or49a, two receptors involved in sensing wasp odors (Ebrahim et al., 2015), into aversion (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Ebrahim et al., 2015.

claim: Hunger does not have a broadly amplifying effect on single-ORN valence.
source: Overall, hunger does not have a broadly amplifying effect on single-ORN valence.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Eight ORN driver lines (three positive, two negative, and three neutral) were crossed to generate seven, two-way ORN combinations.
source: We crossed eight ORN driver lines (three positive, two negative, and three neutral) so as to generate seven, two-way ORN combinations (henceforth 'ORN-combos').
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.

claim: Compared to their constituent single ORNs, the ORN-combos elicited distinct valences.
source: Compared to their constituent single ORNs, the ORN-combos elicited distinct valences (Figure 5A, B and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in figures.

claim: Regression showed that none of the three functions (summation, min-pooling, and max-pooling) could account for a large proportion of ORN-combo valence: summation, min-pooling, and max-pooling all had coefficients of determination of ~0.2 or lower.
source: Strikingly, regression showed that none of the three functions could account for a large proportion of ORN-combo valence: summation, min-pooling, and max-pooling all had coefficients of determination of ~0.2 or lower (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis results presented in a figure supplement.

claim: Bland-Altman method-comparison plots revealed wide limits of agreement (LoAs) between the observed and predicted ORN-combo valences by all three models: summation [SD1.96–0.45, 0.28], max-pooling [SD1.96–0.34, 0.13], min-pooling [SD1.96–0.1, 0.35].
source: Furthermore, Bland-Altman method-comparison plots revealed wide limits of agreement (LoAs) between the observed and predicted ORN-combo valences by all three models: summation [SD1.96–0.45, 0.28], max-pooling [SD1.96–0.34, 0.13], min-pooling [SD1.96–0.1, 0.35] (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis results presented in a figure supplement.

claim: None of the three simple pooling rules (summation, max-pooling, min-pooling) are major predictors of how two-ORN odor valence emerges from single-ORN valence.
source: This analysis thus demonstrates that none of these three simple pooling rules are major predictors of how two-ORN odor valence emerges from single-ORN valence.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data analysis results.

claim: As the light intensity increased, the β points shifted further away from the diagonal.
source: Moreover, as the light intensity increased, the β points shifted further away from the diagonal (Figure 5J) and, in some cases, flipped dominance (Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis results presented in figures.

claim: For ORN-type pairs, increasing intensity is associated with two phenomena: one of the two ORNs tends to become more dominant; and the combination rules are different at different activity levels.
source: For these ORN-type pairs, increasing intensity is associated with two phenomena: one of the two ORNs tends to become more dominant; and the combination rules are different at different activity levels.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The interactions between pairs of ORN types vary depending on receptor identity and stimulus intensity.
source: Thus, the interactions between ORN pairs vary depending on receptor identity and stimulus intensity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: A multiple linear regression (MLR) model with eight LVs had the best performance, with an adjusted coefficient of determination (R2adj) of 0.23.
source: A multiple linear regression (MLR) model with eight LVs had the best performance, with an adjusted coefficient of determination (R2adj) of 0.23.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis results.

claim: The low R2adj score indicates that linear combinations of the available ORN-activity patterns are only weakly predictive of valence.
source: While the two-dimensional space defined by the first two LVs supports a partial separation of aversive and attractive odors (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B), the low R2adj score indicates that linear combinations of the available ORN-activity patterns are only weakly predictive of valence.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data analysis results.

claim: Valence-weighting improved the R2adj of the MLR model from 0.23 to 0.33, but the predictive performances of the models were not improved.
source: Although valence-weighting improved the R2adj of the MLR model from 0.23 to 0.33, the predictive performances of the models were not improved (Supplementary file 2 - Sheet 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis results.

claim: Linear combinations of ORN activity can only account for a minority of odor preference.
source: This further supports the hypothesis that linear combinations of ORN activity can only account for a minority of odor preference.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data analysis results.

claim: 10/45 of single ORN-types have the ability to influence locomotor preference.
source: The screen results indicate that 10/45 of single ORN-types have the ability to influence locomotor preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the screen.

claim: Most ORN types are not individually valent.
source: Thus, most ORN types are not individually valent.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The screen identified four novel valent ORNs (85d, 59c, 35a, 47a) with ligands and ecological roles yet to be determined.
source: The screen identified four novel valent ORNs (85d, 59 c, 35 a, 47 a) with ligands and ecological roles yet to be determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the screen.

claim: Around 60% of pure odorants are valent.
source: Around 60% of pure odorants are valent (Knaden et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Knaden et al., 2012.

claim: At least three of the known valent ORN classes (those for geosmin, CO2, and cVA) are specialized to bind specific ligands exclusively.
source: while at least three of the known valent ORN classes (those for geosmin, CO2, and cVA) are specialized to bind specific ligands exclusively.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about these receptors.

claim: The disconnect between a preponderance of valent odorants (~60% of odorants) and the scarcity of broadly tuned, valent ORN types (≤ 15%) implies that most olfactory valence arises from combined activity in multiple ORN classes.
source: This disconnect between a preponderance of valent odorants (~60% of odorants) and the scarcity of broadly tuned, valent ORN types ( ≤ 15%) implies that most olfactory valence arises from combined activity in multiple ORN classes (Mathew et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results and supported by citations.

claim: Broad activation across ~70% of ORNs drives strong attraction.
source: This idea is also supported by the Orco activation result showing that broad activation across ~70% of ORNs drives strong attraction.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Olfactory neurons elicit valence without airflow, and wind has little to no amplifying effect.
source: However, our experiments showed that olfactory neurons elicit valence without airflow, and that wind has little to no amplifying effect (Figures 1C and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in figures.

claim: Drosophila larvae display both olfactory behavior and optogenetic ORN valence in still air.
source: Note also that even though Drosophila larvae behavioral tests are routinely performed in still air, they display both olfactory behavior and optogenetic ORN valence (Bellmann et al., 2010; Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015; Mathew et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Drosophila ORNs influence valence behavior even without wind.
source: Thus, the overall evidence indicates that Drosophila ORNs influence valence behavior even without wind.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results and prior studies.

claim: Hunger has been reported to increase olfactory attraction.
source: A second factor, hunger, has also been reported to increase olfactory attraction (Gelperin, 1971; Ko et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In the single-ORN screen, starvation had modest effects on valence.
source: However, in the single-ORN screen, starvation had modest effects on valence (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The difference in olfactory responses between fed and starved animals might only be pronounced for weaker olfactory stimuli.
source: First, the difference in olfactory responses between fed and starved animals might only be pronounced for weaker olfactory stimuli: one study showed that the ethyl acetate (EA) response difference between fed and starved flies declines as the EA concentration increases (Chakraborty, 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation supported by a citation to Chakraborty, 2010.

claim: Five vinegar-responsive ORNs are modulated by hunger only when activated in concert, but not when they are activated in subsets.
source: One study found that five vinegar-responsive ORNs are modulated by hunger only when activated in concert, but not when they are activated in subsets (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Root et al., 2011.

claim: The absence of hunger amplification in single-ORN valence—and its presence in female Orco valence—suggests that the potentiating effects of hunger on olfactory attraction might only operate on multi-ORN stimuli like Orco activation and natural odors.
source: The absence of hunger amplification in single-ORN valence—and its presence in female Orco valence—also suggests that the potentiating effects of hunger on olfactory attraction might only operate on multi-ORN stimuli like Orco activation and natural odors.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from the experimental results.

claim: Most odor-guided locomotion arises from the broad activation of ORNs simultaneously.
source: Together, the single-ORN results support the idea that most odor-guided locomotion arises from the broad activation of ORNs simultaneously.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: In a model of Drosophila larval olfaction, the weighted summation of ORN activity in just five of 21 receptors could be used to predict odor valence.
source: In a model of Drosophila larval olfaction, the weighted summation of ORN activity in just five of 21 receptors could be used to predict odor valence (Kreher et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kreher et al., 2008.

claim: An optogenetic study of ORNs reported that combination valences could be explained by summation and/or max-pooling.
source: In adults, an optogenetic study of ORNs reported that combination valences could be explained by summation and/or max-pooling (Bell and Wilson, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bell and Wilson, 2016.

claim: The ORN combinations have diverse, intermediate valence weights within the weight space.
source: Rather, the ORN combinations have diverse, intermediate valence weights within the weight space.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The ORN combination weights shift as the stimulus intensity increases, and appear to even swap dominancy at different intensities.
source: Moreover, these weights shift as the stimulus intensity increases, and appear to even swap dominancy at different intensities.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The variability of β values across a range of stimuli indicates that single-ORNs can contribute a dynamic range of weights when co-activated.
source: The variability of β values across a range of stimuli indicates that (1) single-ORNs can contribute a dynamic range of weights when co-activated
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Many ORN combinations likely share downstream targets.
source: and (3) that many ORN combinations likely share downstream targets.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The underlying neural network is multifactorial and perhaps context-specific.
source: Therefore, we can cautiously infer that the underlying neural network is multifactorial (Qiu et al., 2021) and perhaps context-specific.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results and supported by a citation.

claim: The increasing dominance of one ORN observed in some of the pairs suggests competitive, antagonistic interactions between channels, such as those mediated by broad lateral synaptic inhibition or ephaptic inhibition between neighboring ORNs.
source: The increasing dominance of one ORN observed in some of the pairs suggests competitive, antagonistic interactions between channels, such as those mediated by broad lateral synaptic inhibition (Olsen and Wilson, 2008) or ephaptic inhibition between neighboring ORNs (Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from the experimental results and supported by citations.

claim: The earlier study used Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), which requires intense blue light (up to 1500 µW/mm2) that adds significant heat and elicits strong responses in the fly visual system.
source: As Chrimson was not available at the time, the earlier study used Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), which requires intense blue light (up to 1500 µW/mm2) that adds significant heat and elicits strong responses in the fly visual system (Supplementary file 2 - Sheet 3).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about the properties of ChR2 and comparison to prior studies.

claim: The present study used the Chrimson channel, which requires lower light intensity and a red wavelength to which the fly eye is less receptive.
source: First, it was able to make use of the Chrimson channel, which requires lower light intensity and a red wavelength to which the fly eye is less receptive.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design of the present study.

claim: All non-optogenetic effects were accounted for with balanced experimental, driver, and responder groups (N = ~ 5148 in each group).
source: Second, all non-optogenetic effects were accounted for with balanced experimental, driver, and responder groups (N = ~ 5148 in each group).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design of the present study.

claim: The use of narrow chambers effectively canalizes fly locomotion into one dimension.
source: First, the use of narrow chambers effectively canalizes fly locomotion into one dimension (Bell and Wilson, 2016; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and is supported by citations.

claim: Optogenetic light is not equivalent to odor stimulation: there may be differences in firing rate, response dynamics, or other features of ORN stimulation.
source: Third, optogenetic light is not equivalent to odor stimulation: there may be differences in firing rate, response dynamics, or other features of ORN stimulation that mean these data are not directly generalizable to odor-elicited activity.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: Published recordings from optogenetic and odor stimuli suggest an approximately five-fold difference in firing rates in some cases.
source: published recordings from optogenetic and odor stimuli suggest an approximately five-fold difference in firing rates in some cases (Bell and Wilson, 2016; Hallem and Carlson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The physiological-activity patterns in projection neurons have been reported to be at least partially predictive of odor valence.
source: Indeed, the physiological-activity patterns in projection neurons have been reported to be at least partially predictive of odor valence (Badel et al., 2016; Knaden et al., 2012; Parnas et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Linear models of ORN activity data could account for a minor fraction of olfactory-behavior variance, and this was not substantially improved with single-class ORN valence information.
source: To examine this, we modeled published ORN activity and valence data sets, finding that linear models of ORN activity data could account for a minor fraction of olfactory-behavior variance, and this was not substantially improved with single-class ORN valence information.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis results.

claim: All the observations in the present study point to a minimal role for simple pooling rules, and support the idea that odor valence is primarily governed by complex circuit dynamics.
source: All the observations in the present study point to a minimal role for simple pooling rules, and support the idea that odor valence is primarily governed by complex circuit dynamics.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from all the experimental results.
